lead: The low noise amplifier (LNA) is the first active block after the antenna and its band filter. It must add as little noise as possible, give enough gain to hide the noise of the mixer behind it, stay linear when strong signals arrive, and be stable with any antenna. Its input is a compromise: the source impedance that gives the lowest noise is usually not the one that gives a perfect power match. Every phone, GPS receiver and base station starts with one.
prereq: You need: the Friis formula and sensitivity from noise figure, reflection coefficient Γ and the Smith chart from transmission lines, and S-parameters from microwave components.

sections.h3: Noise match is not power match

blocks.text: The LNA's noise figure adds almost directly to the receiver's, because the first stage dominates the Friis sum, so 1 dB saved here is about 1 dB of sensitivity. Every transistor has four noise parameters: the minimum noise factor F<sub>min</sub>, the source reflection coefficient Γ<sub>opt</sub> at which F<sub>min</sub> is reached, and the equivalent noise resistance R<sub>n</sub>, which says how fast F rises as the source reflection Γ<sub>s</sub> moves away from Γ<sub>opt</sub>:

blocks.where: F and F<sub>min</sub> are linear noise factors (convert to dB only at the end, NF = 10 log₁₀F); R<sub>n</sub> in Ω; Z₀ is the reference impedance, usually 50 Ω; Γ<sub>s</sub> and Γ<sub>opt</sub> are complex reflection coefficients.

blocks.text: On a Smith chart points of equal F form circles around Γ<sub>opt</sub>. Maximum power transfer needs Γ<sub>s</sub> = Γ<sub>in</sub>*, generally elsewhere, so a pure noise match can leave a return loss of only 6 to 12 dB. Designers pick a Γ<sub>s</sub> between the two, or use inductive degeneration, which moves the power-match point close to Γ<sub>opt</sub>.
The standard narrowband CMOS LNA is a common-source MOSFET with an inductor L<sub>s</sub> in its source and an inductor L<sub>g</sub> in series with its gate. Its input impedance is

blocks.where: g<sub>m</sub> is the transconductance in S; C<sub>gs</sub> the gate-source capacitance in F; ω<sub>T</sub> = g<sub>m</sub>/C<sub>gs</sub> is the transit frequency in rad/s (the datasheet value f<sub>T</sub> = ω<sub>T</sub>/2π is in Hz).

blocks.text: The real part ω<sub>T</sub>L<sub>s</sub> is made by feedback through L<sub>s</sub>, not by a resistor, so it adds no thermal noise of its own. The design takes two steps: choose L<sub>s</sub> = 50/ω<sub>T</sub> so that Re Z<sub>in</sub> = 50 Ω, then choose L<sub>g</sub> so that L<sub>g</sub> + L<sub>s</sub> resonates with C<sub>gs</sub> at the operating frequency ω₀, that is (L<sub>g</sub> + L<sub>s</sub>) = 1/(ω₀²C<sub>gs</sub>). At resonance the gate voltage is Q<sub>in</sub> times the source voltage, with Q<sub>in</sub> = 1/(2R<sub>s</sub>ω₀C<sub>gs</sub>) for a source R<sub>s</sub>, so the stage's effective transconductance is g<sub>m</sub>Q<sub>in</sub> = ω<sub>T</sub>/(2ω₀R<sub>s</sub>).

A cascode transistor stacked on top (common-gate) cuts the Miller feedback from drain to gate, so the input match does not depend on the load and reverse isolation is high. Its own noise, referred to the input, is divided by the gain of the first device, so it adds little. The cost is headroom: two drain-source voltages must fit under the supply. A tuned LC load or a matching network sets the output match and the gain.

An LNA needs just enough gain, typically 12 to 20 dB: enough to make the mixer's term (F₂ − 1)/G₁ small, not so much that the stages after it compress first; cascaded IIP3 falls as G₁ rises. Output values follow from input values by adding G: P1dB,out = P1dB,in + G − 1 and OIP3 = IIP3 + G.
The LNA must not oscillate with any passive source or load. With S-parameters, Δ = S₁₁S₂₂ − S₁₂S₂₁ and the Rollett factor

blocks.where: K > 1 together with |Δ| < 1 means unconditionally stable at that frequency; check it at every frequency where the device has gain.

examples.question: Design the input of an inductively degenerated CMOS LNA for 2.4 GHz and a 50 Ω source. The transistor has g<sub>m</sub> = 60 mS and C<sub>gs</sub> = 300 fF. Find ω<sub>T</sub>, f<sub>T</sub>, L<sub>s</sub>, L<sub>g</sub>, Q<sub>in</sub>, the effective transconductance and the input return loss at 2.3 and 2.5 GHz.
steps: ω<sub>T</sub> = g<sub>m</sub>/C<sub>gs</sub> = 0.06/(300 × 10⁻¹⁵) = 2.0 × 10¹¹ rad/s; f<sub>T</sub> = ω<sub>T</sub>/2π = 31.8 GHz.
L<sub>s</sub> = 50/ω<sub>T</sub> = 50/(2 × 10¹¹) = 0.25 nH (a bond wire or a short on-chip line).
L<sub>g</sub> = 14.66 − 0.25 = 14.41 nH, too large for a good on-chip spiral, so it is usually an off-chip inductor or part of the package.
At 2.4 GHz, 1/(ω₀C<sub>gs</sub>) = 221 Ω; Q<sub>in</sub> = 221/(50 + 50) = 2.21. Effective transconductance = g<sub>m</sub>Q<sub>in</sub> = 60 × 2.21 = 132.6 mS.

At 2.3 GHz: Z<sub>in</sub> = 50 − j18.8 Ω, |Γ| = 0.185, return loss 14.7 dB. At 2.5 GHz: Z<sub>in</sub> = 50 + j18.1 Ω, |Γ| = 0.178, return loss 15.0 dB. The whole 2.4 GHz band is matched better than 10 dB.
examples.answer: ω<sub>T</sub> = 2 × 10¹¹ rad/s (f<sub>T</sub> = 31.8 GHz), L<sub>s</sub> = 0.25 nH, L<sub>g</sub> = 14.41 nH, Q<sub>in</sub> = 2.21, effective g<sub>m</sub> = 132.6 mS, return loss about 15 dB at ±100 MHz.

examples.question: A transistor at 2.4 GHz has F<sub>min</sub> = 1.0 dB, R<sub>n</sub> = 8 Ω and Γ<sub>opt</sub> = 0.5∠45°; its input reflection is Γ<sub>in</sub> = 0.6∠−60°. Find the noise figure (a) with a plain 50 Ω source, (b) with a noise match and (c) with a power match, and the input return loss for each.
steps: (a) Γ<sub>s</sub> = 0: |Γ<sub>s</sub> − Γ<sub>opt</sub>|² = 0.25; F = 1.259 + 0.64 × 0.25/1.957 = 1.259 + 0.082 = 1.341, NF = 1.27 dB. Reflection = |Γ<sub>in</sub>| = 0.6, return loss 4.4 dB.
(b) Γ<sub>s</sub> = Γ<sub>opt</sub>: NF = F<sub>min</sub> = 1.00 dB. The reflection at the input is |(Γ<sub>in</sub> − Γ<sub>s</sub>*)/(1 − Γ<sub>in</sub>Γ<sub>s</sub>)| = 0.244, return loss 12.2 dB.
The power match costs only 0.05 dB of noise figure here because Γ<sub>in</sub>* lies close to Γ<sub>opt</sub>; a plain 50 Ω source costs 0.27 dB and a 4.4 dB return loss.
examples.answer: 50 Ω source: 1.27 dB and 4.4 dB return loss; noise match: 1.00 dB and 12.2 dB; power match: 1.05 dB and a perfect match. Choose the power match or a point between.

traps: Putting F<sub>min</sub> in dB into the noise-parameter formula. The formula works in linear factors; 1.0 dB is F<sub>min</sub> = 1.259.
Assuming Γ<sub>opt</sub> = Γ<sub>in</sub>*. The lowest-noise source and the matched source are different points, so lowest NF does not mean lowest reflection.
Taking ω<sub>T</sub> as f<sub>T</sub>. R<sub>in</sub> = ω<sub>T</sub>L<sub>s</sub> uses rad/s; using f<sub>T</sub> in Hz makes L<sub>s</sub> 2π times too large.
Adding a 50 Ω resistor at the gate to get a match. It matches, but its own noise sets NF above 3 dB; degeneration gives the real part without noise.
Calling an amplifier stable because K > 1. Unconditional stability needs |Δ| < 1 as well, at every frequency with gain.

quiz.q: Name the four noise parameters of a transistor.
quiz.a: F<sub>min</sub>, the magnitude and the angle of Γ<sub>opt</sub>, and R<sub>n</sub>.

quiz.q: How does a source inductor give a real input resistance without adding noise?
quiz.a: Drain current through L<sub>s</sub> feeds back a voltage proportional to the gate current, which makes Z<sub>in</sub> contain the real term ω<sub>T</sub>L<sub>s</sub>. No resistor is involved, so no thermal noise is added.

quiz.q: An LNA has G = 15 dB, P1dB,in = −20 dBm and IIP3 = −10 dBm. Find P1dB,out and OIP3.
A transistor has S₁₁ = 0.6∠−60°, S₂₁ = 4∠80°, S₁₂ = 0.05∠50° and S₂₂ = 0.5∠−40°. Is it unconditionally stable?
quiz.a: Δ = S₁₁S₂₂ − S₁₂S₂₁: |Δ| = 0.455 < 1. K = (1 − 0.36 − 0.25 + 0.207)/(2 × 0.2) = 1.49 > 1. Yes, at this frequency.

quiz.q: An LNA has NF = 1.5 dB and a 10 MHz channel. Find its input noise floor and the sensitivity for SNR<sub>min</sub> = 10 dB.
Give two benefits and one cost of a cascode LNA.
quiz.a: Benefits: high reverse isolation (less Miller feedback), so the input match and stability do not depend on the load; higher output resistance and gain. Cost: extra voltage headroom for the stacked transistor.

quiz.q: Why is more LNA gain not always better?
quiz.a: Gain beyond what hides the mixer noise lowers NF only slightly, but it raises the signal level at the mixer and IF stages, which lowers the cascaded IIP3 and makes the receiver easier to block.

beyond: Not for the exam. Wideband LNAs use noise-cancelling topologies, where the matching transistor's noise cancels at the output while its signal adds. Cryogenic HEMT LNAs reach a few kelvin for radio astronomy and quantum-computer readout. Search for 'noise cancelling LNA' and 'cryogenic HEMT amplifier'.

spec.aria: Circuit of the LNA. A 50 ohm source feeds a 14.41 nanohenry gate inductor into the gate of transistor M1, which has Cgs of 300 femtofarads and gm of 60 millisiemens. M1's source goes to ground through a 0.25 nanohenry inductor. Cascode transistor M2 sits above M1 with a tuned load to the supply, and the output goes to the mixer. A panel lists omega T equals 2 times 10 to the 11 radians per second, real part of Zin equals 50 ohms, Lg plus Ls equals 14.66 nanohenries, Qin of 2.21 and return loss of 15 dB at plus and minus 100 megahertz.
